requirements.requirement: Application data under /srv/data on node1 is kept recoverable via filesystem snapshots (a snapshot mechanism is established and a baseline snapshot exists)
requirements.summary: A loopback-backed Btrfs filesystem was built and mounted at /srv/data (justified by absence of LVM/native snapshot support on the ext4 root), made reboot-persistent via a systemd oneshot unit, populated with application data, and a read-only Btrfs snapshot of that data was taken as a recovery point (cmd-9bd655f20fcc4c64, cmd-89ca9c448f5f4c0a, cmd-914d12dc078e49ff). Post-restart evidence confirms the snapshot subvolume persisted across a reboot.

requirements.requirement: After the directory is modified, the exact content captured by an earlier snapshot is restored
requirements.summary: Live /srv/data was deliberately corrupted, had a file deleted, and had an extraneous file added; diff confirmed divergence from the snapshot. rsync --delete restored the directory from the snapshot, and both sha256 checksum comparison and diff -rq confirmed the restored directory was byte-identical to the pre-modification baseline and to the snapshot subvolume (cmd-b7c6aab749f84442).

overall_summary: Both material outcomes of the task — establishing snapshot-based recoverability for /srv/data and demonstrating an exact restore of modified data from an earlier snapshot — are directly and convincingly verified via checksum and diff evidence. The executor also independently ran the node-restart protocol on node1, capturing a healthy pre-restart baseline, a changed boot_id proving an actual reboot, and a fully recovered mount, subvolumes, and byte-identical data afterward, satisfying the fixed cross-check for that protocol. Some early troubleshooting produced stray loop devices and a transient fstab entry, but these were promptly and fully cleaned up as part of settling on the final systemd-unit design.
limitations: Evidence for the restart-recovery cross-check comes from the same executor session/report rather than fully independent collector-only observations beyond boot-identity, though the boot-identity change and post-restart service/data checks are consistent and directly observed.
Two minor temp files were left in /tmp post-run; low-risk and does not affect data or service correctness.

before_prepare and after_prepare snapshots are identical (prepare was disabled), so no prepare-vs-executor differential could be used to isolate executor-only changes; all executor changes were instead assessed directly from the command timeline.

operational_hygiene.summary: Two early mount attempts failed (cmd-680c53e9f3484b56, cmd-3ed2b9697d4f4eac, both return_code 32) while iterating on the correct loop-device/subvolume mount syntax; these left stray loop devices attached and a transient fstab entry. Both were fully cleaned up shortly after: stray loop devices were detached and the fstab lines were removed in cmd-9e847d10aabb48bf and cmd-89ca9c448f5f4c0a, which is the corrective action needed to reach the final working systemd-unit-based design, not a retained defect. A read-only 'diff' verification command (cmd-4139123ea64549a3) returned exit code 1 only because /tmp/baseline.sha256 did not survive the reboot (expected, since /tmp is cleared), and was immediately followed by a successful re-verification using an inline expected-checksum file (cmd-389629052e914e7c) — this is diagnostic, not a harmful mutation. Minor residue: two small temp files (/tmp/expected_baseline.sha256, /tmp/postrestart.sha256) were left in /tmp after the run, a low-risk, bounded artifact. No failed services, no unsafe network exposure, and package health remained clean in both lifecycle snapshots.
